figures.caption: Fig. 1. Two common positions for evaluating the medial elbow with ultrasonography. Open in a new tab A. The seated position and probe placement enable a rapid and straightforward examination of the medial elbow in the long axis. B. The supine position and probe placement provide greater comfort for dynamic assessment.

Fig. 2. Normal long-axis ultrasound (US) image of the medial elbow and corresponding magnetic resonance (MR) image. Open in a new tab The long-axis US image (A) and the corresponding MR fat-suppressed proton density coronal image (B) display the normal appearance of the common flexor tendon (double-headed arrow) and muscle (m). The anterior band of the ulnar collateral ligament (arrowheads) is situated deep to the common flexor tendon, extending from the medial epicondyle (ME) to the sublime tubercle of the ulna (U).

Fig. 3. Normal short-axis ultrasound (US) image of the posteromedial elbow and corresponding magnetic resonance (MR) image. Open in a new tab The short-axis US image (A) and the corresponding MR T2-weighted axial image (B) display the normal appearance of the cubital tunnel and the ulnar nerve. The cubital tunnel is a fibro-osseous channel that lies between the medial epicondyle (ME) and the olecranon (O). This structure is covered by the cubital tunnel retinaculum (arrowheads), with the posterior band (arrows) of the ulnar collateral ligament forming its floor. Within the cubital tunnel, the ulnar nerve (asterisk) exhibits a normal fascicular pattern with hypoechoic neural bundles. A, anconeus; P, pronator teres.

Fig. 4. Ultrasound (US) findings of medial epicondylitis. Open in a new tab A. Long-axis US images of the medial elbow in a 55-year-old woman reveal swelling, hypoechoic change, and outward bowing of the common flexor tendon (arrowheads). B. Doppler US image of the same patient displays neovascularization in the tendon. C. Long-axis view of the medial elbow in a 63-year-old man shows a small calcification (arrow) in the common flexor tendon and a focal low-echoic area, indicative of a small tendon tear (arrowheads). ME, medial epicondyle.

Fig. 5. Radiograph and ultrasound (US) images of a 61-year-old woman with calcific tendinitis of the common flexor tendon. Open in a new tab A. Oblique radiograph of the elbow reveals fluffy and cloudy calcifications (arrows) at the insertion of the common flexor tendon near the medial epicondyle (ME) of the humerus. B. Long-axis US image of the medial elbow displays an amorphous calcific deposit within the common flexor tendon, exhibiting minimal posterior acoustic shadowing. U, ulna; R, radius.

Fig. 6. Schematic drawing depicting common sites of ulnar nerve entrapment. Open in a new tab The Osborne band (fascia) is shown as the fascia that covers the humeral and ulnar heads of the flexor carpi ulnaris, as originally described. The cubital tunnel retinaculum, which is distinct from the Osborne fascia, forms the roof of the cubital tunnel.

Fig. 7. Ultrasound images of the posteromedial elbow at the level of the cubital tunnel in a 25-year-old woman with ulnar neuropathy. Open in a new tab A. Short-axis view at the cubital tunnel reveals a hypoechoic, enlarged ulnar nerve (asterisk) situated between the medial epicondyle (ME) and the olecranon (O). The cross-sectional area of the ulnar nerve is 10.4 mm 2 . The cubital tunnel retinaculum (arrowheads) is visible as a hyperechoic membranous structure covering the cubital tunnel. B. Long-axis view of the cubital tunnel demonstrates segmental enlargement of the ulnar nerve (asterisk) at the proximal cubital tunnel, while the distal ulnar nerve exhibits a normal hyperechoic fascicular appearance (arrows).

Fig. 8. Patient positioning and probe placement for ulnar nerve instability testing, along with corresponding ultrasound images. Open in a new tab A. By placing the transducer at the cubital tunnel with minimal pressure, the examiner can observe whether the ulnar nerve displaces from the cubital tunnel upon elbow flexion. B-D. Short-axis ultrasound images obtained at the posteromedial elbow demonstrate the ulnar nerve in various positions during elbow flexion. B. In a 28-year-old man, the ulnar nerve (asterisk) is located posterior to the medial epicondyle (ME), which is its typical position during elbow flexion. C. In a 29-year-old woman, the ulnar nerve (asterisk) is subluxated at the apex of the ME during elbow flexion. D. In a 58-year-old man, the ulnar nerve (asterisk) is completely dislocated and positioned anterior to the ME during elbow flexion. Tri, triceps brachii.

Fig. 9. Dynamic ultrasound images of a 22-year-old man with snapping medial triceps syndrome. Open in a new tab A. Short-axis view of the posteromedial elbow in extension reveals the ulnar nerve (asterisk) located posterior to the medial epicondyle (ME). B. Short-axis view of the flexed elbow demonstrates dislocation of the ulnar nerve (asterisk) anterior to the ME. C. Short-axis view of the fully flexed elbow illustrates subluxation of the medial triceps muscle belly (arrows) over the ME pushing the ulnar nerve (asterisk) anteriorly. Tri, triceps brachii.

Fig. 10. A 27-year-old man who presented with right medial elbow pain that arose while he was doing push-ups. Open in a new tab The patient had a history of right medial elbow injury sustained during gymnastics in middle school. A. Dynamic ultrasound (US) with valgus stress can be performed with the patient’s arm abducted and the elbow flexed. The US probe should visualize the ulnar collateral ligament and medial joint space while the examiner applies a valgus force by pressing down on the patient’s forearm or hand to expand the medial joint space of the elbow. B-E. Dynamic US images with valgus stress on the bilateral elbow are presented for comparison. B. Long-axis image of the normal left medial elbow shows the ulnar collateral ligament (arrows) with a low-echoic appearance due to anisotropy artifact. C. When valgus stress is applied, the ulnar collateral ligament (arrows) straightens, appears hyperechoic, and demonstrates a normal fibrillar appearance. Note that the medial joint space shows little change with valgus stress. D. Long-axis image obtained from the injured right medial elbow reveals thickening and a low-echoic change in the ulnar collateral ligament (arrows). E. With valgus stress applied, the medial joint space expands, with a joint space difference of more than 2 mm. Note the focal sagging (arrowhead) of the overlying flexor muscle into the widened joint space, indicating discontinuity of the ulnar collateral ligament. ME, medial epicondyle; U, ulna.

Fig. 11. Schematic representation of the anatomy, ultrasound (US) probe placement, and corresponding US image of the medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve at the right elbow. Open in a new tab A. The medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve runs alongside the basilic vein and medial to the biceps muscle, which can serve as a landmark for locating the nerve. B. Corresponding US image displays the biceps brachii muscle (Biceps), brachialis, brachial vein (V), brachial artery (A), median nerve (M), and anterior branch of the medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve (dotted line).

Fig. 12. A 51-year-old woman who presented with right elbow pain. Open in a new tab A. Short-axis view at the posteromedial elbow reveals a distended posteromedial synovial recess between the medial epicondyle (ME) and olecranon (O), accompanied by effusion (E) and synovial hypertrophy (arrowheads). B. Longitudinal Doppler ultrasound view of the anterolateral elbow demonstrates mass-like synovial thickening (arrowheads) with hyperemia in the elbow joint. C, capitellum; R, radius.

Fig. 13. A 15-year-old boy who presented with a painful mass at the medial elbow, diagnosed as Kimura lymphadenopathy. Open in a new tab A. Short-axis ultrasound image reveals an irregularly shaped, hypoechoic mass (asterisk) with vascularity in the subcutaneous layer of the medial epitrochlear area. B. Corresponding T1-weighted magnetic resonance image displays a mass (asterisk) with low signal intensity situated adjacent to the basilic vein (B) in the epitrochlear area, strongly indicative of lymph node enlargement.
